$comment: The protocol version both sides must agree on, plus conformance cases for the `GET /api/v1/version` payload. `protocol_version` is the assertion that matters: server/tests/test_protocol_fixtures.py checks it against fenixspoon.protocol.PROTOCOL_VERSION and the SDK's conformance suite checks it against PROTOCOL_VERSION in @fenix-spoon/client, so bumping one side without the other fails CI on the other. 1.1 added vector fields to both result kinds; 1.2 added the discovery operations (/environment, /capabilities, /capabilities/{name}, /capabilities/{name}/schema) and their payloads — both additive, so 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 share /api/v1. 1.3 added `metrics` and `diagnostics` to the result envelope, plus the compact `/jobs/{id}/summary` and `/jobs/{id}/query` routes; the heat adapters' `t_max` and `t_rise` moved out of `stats` into `metrics` in the same bump, which is additive because `stats` keys have always been documented as server-defined and all optional. 1.4 added the content-addressed result cache (#47): `provenance` on the result envelope and as a compact level, `cached` on the submit response, and real cache state in `environment.inspect`. Additive, but note one behavioural change a client can see — `POST /jobs` may return a job that is already `done`. 1.5 added the `series1d` result kind and the `series` key beside `data` (#69), the `assumptions` section on `capability.describe` (#70), and the `series` level on `/jobs/{id}/summary`; the potential-flow adapters gained `circulation`, `c_l`, `c_m_c4` and `x_cp` in the same release (#68), which needs no bump of its own because `metrics` keys have always been whatever a capability declares. It is 1.5 rather than a second 1.4 because #47 reached main first and the rule below applies to it as much as to 1.2. Unlike the 1.2 discovery payloads, the series half *is* validated on both sides: a curve has a browser consumer, so there is a second implementation to drift from — and `series_limits` in results.json pins its ceilings the way `protocol_version` pins this. The `workspace` path in the environment payload is part of 1.2 rather than a 1.3: #43 specified the field and had nothing to point at, #44 built the workspace, and both land unreleased on the same branch. Folding it in is only correct while 1.2 is unmerged — once a version is on main it is fixed, and the next addition is a bump. When a MAJOR arrives, this file gains a `superseded` list and the corpus holds cases for both. 1.6 added `over` to a declared metric (#86): `payload` (the default, and what every steady capability means) or `run` for a quantity only the adapter can supply — a peak over a transient's history, a time to reach a level. Additive, and a discovery-payload change like 1.2's, so the SDK carries the version but models nothing new. 1.7 gave an artifact an optional `t` and the result envelope a derived `frames` list (#86): the time index of a transient is the artifacts carrying an instant, in time order. Additive, and deliberately not a new result kind — the field history crosses as references like every other large thing, and there is no server-side reduction at a chosen instant. Deriving the index from the files rather than storing it beside them is what makes a frame naming a file the result does not serve unrepresentable. Unlike 1.6, the SDK does model this one: `ArtifactRef.t` and `FrameRef` are part of the result envelope it already types, so leaving them out would have made the version constant advertise a shape the types denied. 1.8 let a geometry *name* pieces of its boundary (#85): optional stable `point_ids` on a polygon, and a `boundaries` list whose selectors are topological (`part`), by point id, or geometric (`near`/`box`/`all_of`). Additive and empty by default — every adapter shipped today puts its conditions where the outer/obstacle split implies them. Ids and predicates are both here because they follow different things: an id follows the shape through an edit, a predicate follows the space. What happens *on* a named boundary is a load case, and lands separately. 1.9 said what happens *on* a named boundary, which 1.8 could only point at (#85): a `load_case` workspace object whose body is `{boundary: {key: value}}`, `conditions` on a submission for the inline form, and a `conditions` section on `capability.describe` listing the keys a capability reads and their units. Additive on the wire, and the values are an open map of scalars exactly like `Region2D.material` — a typed enum of condition kinds would put physics into the protocol and make every new physics a protocol change. What keeps that openness honest is the capability declaration: a key nothing declares, or a boundary the geometry does not name, is a 422 at submit rather than a silent no-op, and all three refusals are in errors.json with the rest of the partition. Two things a caller should know beyond the additions. The `load_case` object body is now *validated*, where before it was stored as given — the same tightening #48 applied to `study`, and the same reasoning: a body gets a schema at the moment something reads it. And a load case is part of a solve's content address, so two load cases on one shape are two cache entries; leaving them out would have served the clamped answer to the caller who asked about the free one. The SDK models this one rather than merely tracking it, as it did for 1.7 and for the same reason: `JobRequest` is a shape it already types, and a version constant that advertised `conditions` while the types denied it would be the drift this file exists to prevent. 1.10 bound the workspace to HTTP (ADR 0002): objects as a resource collection under /objects/{type}/{id} with the revision as a query parameter, and `design` on a job submission so a browser can solve by reference rather than resending its geometry. Additive — every route is new and `POST /jobs` still accepts the inline form — so 1.10 shares /api/v1 with 1.0. Note the version string itself: this is the first minor that breaks both a float comparison and a lexicographic one, and the corpus carries a case for it above. 1.11 added the two study routes (ADR 0002 decision 3): POST /studies/{id}/run and GET /studies/{id}. A study is an object that runs rather than an endpoint that computes, so there is no request body — everything the run needs is in the revision it names. Additive.

valid.name: a later minor on the same major
valid.$comment: Additive, so a 1.0 client must still accept it.

valid.name: a two-digit minor
valid.$comment: 1.10, and the first case in this corpus that exists to break naive comparisons rather than to exercise a shape. As a float it parses to 1.1 and sorts below 1.9; as a string it *also* sorts below "1.9", because '1' < '9' at the third character. The document has warned about the first since 1.0 and not about the second, and a draft of ADR 0002 proposed pinning `"1.10" > "1.9"` as a test — an assertion that is false, written by someone who had read the warning. Split on the dot and compare the halves as integers, which is what checkProtocolCompatibility does.

invalid.name: missing protocol
invalid.reason: protocol is required: a payload that cannot say what it speaks is useless

invalid.name: missing api_path
invalid.reason: api_path is required so a client can confirm where this version is served

invalid.name: protocol as a number
invalid.reason: MAJOR.MINOR is a string; as a float 1.10 would compare below 1.9. Note pydantic v2 refuses this on type alone — it does not coerce numbers to str — so this case guards the rule, not a coercion bug.

invalid.name: protocol with a non-numeric minor
invalid.reason: MAJOR.MINOR must be two integers; '1.banana' cannot be compared with anything

invalid.name: protocol with only a major
invalid.reason: '1' leaves the minor implicit, and an implicit minor is a guess
